newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close little changed, digest auction.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close little changed, digest auction.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed little changed in light, rangebound trade on Tuesday as players digested the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding effort, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended off 1/32 at 97-11/32. Its yield rose a notch to 6.71 percent from the 6.70 percent seen at Monday's close.
The Treasury sold $17.754 billion in three-year notes at an average yield of 5.997 percent. The bid-to-cover ratio in the auction was 2.22 to one.

Demand for the securities was called "fairly good" by several traders in the market. They said the auction was led mostly by foreign central banks and Wall Street dealers, perceived as heavy bidders at the sale.
"The three-year note auction came in right on the screws where it was supposed to come," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities.

Retailers as well as portfolio managers were perceived to be mostly out of the auction. Some players said they noticed a little hedge fund bidding shortly before the sale's deadline at 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
Although the three-year notes were smoothly placed on Tuesday, analysts expressed some concern about the two remaining auctions in the quarterly refunding effort.

Analysts said recent comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin saying the dollar has been strong "for some time" cast doubt on the future of the greenback and, as a result, discouraged some players to bid in the refunding auctions.
"The market's rally has sort of run into a wall ever since Rubin's comments on Friday set the negative tone heading into the refunding. We've been trading sideways since then," Dimick said.

"To me that suggests a loss of momentum which is dangerous going into the longer maturity segments of the refunding," the UBS Treasury strategist added. The Treasury will offer $12.0 billion in 10-year securities on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Traders also said Treasury is raising a lot of new cash at the refunding since there is a lot of new issuance, but, they noted, there are not a lot of securities maturing.
Market experts estimated that nearly $21.0 billion out of a total of $39.75 billion in new securities being sold at the refunding is new cash.
"That means you're asking a lot of people to come up with new money to buy these papers," said a trader at a U.S. major investment bank.
The market paid little attention to the new economic data released on Tuesday. A 2.2 percent jump in non-farm productivity in the fourth quarter of 1996 was mostly shrugged off by players.
The market also took in a drop in the Richmond Federal Reserve Bank's manufacturing shipments index to -9.0 in January from -2.0 in December.

"The Fed will sit on its hands for the time being. But I must say that we continue to build into our internal and external forecasts a (tightening) move in May," said Wayne Ayers, chief economist at Bank of Boston.
"Not because necessaryly we think the economic numbers are going to be so boomy. But we are going to continue to see signs of a tighter labor market," he added.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down one basis point at 5.01 percent. The six-month bill rate fell one point to 5.07 percent. The year bill rate was unchanged at 5.21 percent.
Traders digested a 0.9 percent rise in the seasonally adjusted BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index for the week ended February 8 versus the prior week.
The Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook Retail Sales Index, also released on Tuesday, showed U.S. seasonally adjusted retail sales rose 2.5 percent in the first week of fiscal February versus January.
Analysts said the data released Tuesday did little to change their perception on Federal Reserve monetary policy.

The two-year note closed flat at 100-1/32, yielding 5.86 percent. The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 100-11/32 to yield 6.17 percent. The ten-year note closed down 2/32 at 100-20/32, yielding 6.41 percent.
